summary: Describes using the HMAC construction with the MD5 hash as the authentication mechanism inside IPsec's ESP and AH. It gives the algorithm-specific details that the base IPsec documents leave out. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A secret handshake proves a friend is really your friend. This document describes one kind of secret handshake, built from a scrambling recipe, that computers use to check packets are genuine.

questions: why is hmac-md5 truncated to 96 bits
what key length does hmac-md5-96 use
subtitle: How IPsec ESP and AH use HMAC with MD5, cut to 96 bits, to prove packets are genuine and unaltered.

tldr.problem: The base IPsec specifications for ESP and AH need an algorithm to check that a packet really came from the sender and was not changed on the way.
tldr.mechanism: HMAC-MD5-96 runs the HMAC construction over MD5 with a 128-bit key and keeps the first 96 bits of the 128-bit result as the authenticator.
tldr.outcome: It gives data origin authentication and integrity protection. The RFC notes that MD5 had been shown to be less collision-resistant than first thought, but argues HMAC does not depend on that property.

today: RFC 2403 is a Proposed Standard published in November 1998, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What HMAC-MD5-96 Is For
sections.content:
This memo specifies MD5 (RFC 1321) combined with HMAC (RFC 2104) as a keyed authentication mechanism inside the IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP, RFC 2406) and Authentication Header (AH, RFC 2402). The goal is to make sure a packet is authentic and cannot be modified in transit.

HMAC is a secret key algorithm, so what it proves depends on who knows the key. If only the source and destination know it, a correct HMAC proves the packet was added by the source.
sections.eli5: It is a tamper seal on each packet. Only people who know the shared secret can make a seal that checks out.

sections.title: Algorithm and Mode
sections.content:
MD5 is described in RFC 1321 and HMAC in RFC 2104; HMAC is a framework into which hash algorithms such as MD5 can be inserted. HMAC-MD5-96 works on 64-byte blocks. MD5 already defines its own padding, so no extra padding is needed, and no implicit packet padding as defined in AH is required.

HMAC-MD5 produces a 128-bit value. For ESP and AH, an implementation MUST support truncating it to the first 96 bits. The sender stores the truncated value in the authenticator field. The receiver computes the full 128-bit value and compares its first 96 bits with the stored field. No other authenticator lengths are supported.

96 bits was chosen because it is the default authenticator length in AH and meets the security requirements of RFC 2104.
sections.eli5: The recipe makes a long fingerprint, but only the first part of it is written on the packet. The receiver makes the whole fingerprint and compares just that part.

sections.title: Performance
sections.content:
The RFC quotes the HMAC authors as saying that HMAC performance is essentially that of the underlying hash function. RFC 1810 gives performance analysis and advice on using MD5 in Internet protocols. At the time of writing, the memo says no performance analysis had been done of HMAC or of HMAC combined with MD5.

RFC 2104 also outlines an implementation change that can speed up per-packet work without affecting interoperability.
sections.eli5: The seal costs about as much effort as the scrambling recipe underneath it, and there is a known shortcut that makes it faster.

sections.title: Keying Material
sections.content:
For ESP and AH, a fixed key length of 128 bits MUST be supported, and other key lengths MUST NOT be supported. The RFC bases this on RFC 2104: keys shorter than the authenticator length weaken security, and longer keys do not significantly add strength. The key MUST be generated with a strong pseudo-random function.

No weak keys for HMAC were specified at the time. If any are found later, they must be rejected and replacement keys requested, or a new Security Association negotiated. To give data origin authentication, the key distribution mechanism must hand out unique keys and share them only with the parties in the communication.

The RFC repeats the RFC 2104 advice that periodic key refreshment is a fundamental security practice, even though current attacks do not point to a specific frequency.
sections.eli5: The secret code word must be a fixed length, truly random-looking, and known only to the two friends. Changing it now and then is a good habit.

sections.title: Interaction with the ESP Cipher
sections.content: When ESP also encrypts, the authentication algorithm sits beside a cipher. The RFC says that at the time of writing there were no known issues preventing HMAC-MD5-96 from being used with any specific cipher algorithm.
sections.eli5: The seal works fine no matter which lock-and-key scrambler is used to hide the contents.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The strength of HMAC-MD5-96 rests mainly on HMAC and, to a lesser degree, on MD5. RFC 2104 claims HMAC does not need strong collision resistance, which matters because MD5 had been shown to be much less collision-resistant than first thought. At the time of writing there were no practical cryptographic attacks against HMAC-MD5-96.

For a 64-byte block hash, a birthday attack involving 264 blocks would be infeasible unless the hash were found to have collisions after processing 230 blocks. The RFC adds that HMAC was designed for keyed use from the start, while MD5 was not, and that HMAC with MD5 had held up under scrutiny. Truncating the output is encouraged for specifications that use HMAC, and MD5 could be swapped for another hash such as SHA-1.

As with any algorithm, security also depends on a correct implementation and sound key management. RFC 2202 provides test vectors and example code for checking HMAC-MD5-96 code.
sections.eli5: MD5 alone has some cracks, but the way HMAC uses it does not rely on the cracked part. Even so, it only stays safe if the code is correct and the secret stays secret.

items.title: Stored value
items.text: First 96 bits, in the authenticator field.
